source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Theory of why exploration fails. Detachment: an agent driven by intrinsic reward leaves a frontier after using up its reward there, forgets how to return, and the frontier can be lost. Derailment: the agent that has reached a promising state cannot get back to it, because the same noise that explores also breaks the return.
numbers: Two root causes named. Offered as the reason no intrinsic-motivation method scored above 0 on Pitfall under stochastic evaluation, and why the best of them solved level 1 of Montezuma's Revenge in only 10% of runs.
limits: This is a hypothesis about causes. The Atari results are indirect evidence; there is no direct test of detachment in Atari.
agent_relevance: Keep a list of promising partial results and do not rely on the model drifting back to them. Exploring should be switched off while returning.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Core algorithm in two phases. Phase 1 explore until solved: an archive of cells, each holding a full trajectory, simulator state, score and trajectory length. Pick a cell, return to it, explore with random actions, add new cells. Phase 2 robustify: turn the best trajectory into a policy that works under noise, using the backward algorithm (learning from demonstrations).
numbers: Exploration step: k=100 training frames of random actions, 95% chance to repeat the previous action. No neural network was used in Phase 1 in any experiment.
quote: The fact that entirely random exploration works so well
limits: Phase 1 uses a deterministic, restorable simulator. That is a strong assumption for real tasks.
agent_relevance: The archive entry is (state, path to it, score, length). For us: a partial solution plus the steps that produced it. Random extension was enough, so the archive and the exact return matter more than clever exploring.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Archive update rule. A cell is added when first seen. An existing cell is replaced when the new trajectory has a higher score or is shorter at equal score. When replaced, the selection counters (times chosen, times since progress) are reset so the cell is tried again; the times-visited count is not reset.
numbers: Replacement criterion: higher cumulative score, or same score and shorter. The authors do not rewrite other cells that were built on the old path.
limits: A better path to a cell may break trajectories that were built on top of the old one.
agent_relevance: Keep the best and the shortest route to each class of partial state, and re-open the class when a better route is found.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Cell representation without domain knowledge: convert the frame to grayscale, downscale to 11 x 8 with area interpolation, rescale pixel intensity to integers 0 to 8. Parameters found by grid search. Fast and needs no game knowledge.
numbers: 11 x 8 image, 9 intensity values (0 to 8). On Pitfall this representation found only 22 rooms; the authors say it fails because visually identical screens need different actions (partial observability).
limits: Cell design is a hand-tuned hyperparameter. Too coarse merges different states; too fine stores every frame.
agent_relevance: Our analogue: how we decide two partial solutions are the same state. Too coarse loses diversity; too fine fills the archive.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Montezuma's Revenge, no domain knowledge. Phase 1 solved level 1 in 57% of 100 runs after 1.2 billion game frames (one run reached level 3). Phase 2 robustified policies reached mean score 43,763 (CI 36,718 to 50,196), above the human expert mean 34,900, and solved level 1 with 99.8% success in stochastic tests.
numbers: Phase 1 mean score 57,439 after a mean 640M frames on a single 22-CPU machine. Prior best intrinsic-motivation score about 17,500. Phase 2: 5 policies, about 4.3B frames.
limits: Robustification from a single demonstration succeeded in only 40% of attempts; with 10 demonstrations, 5 of 5 runs succeeded.
agent_relevance: Cheap exploration with an archive beat the dominant method. A single path is fragile; many diverse solved paths make the final step robust (compare: several candidate solutions before a final check).

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Montezuma's Revenge with domain knowledge cells (x,y in 16x16 pixel blocks, room, level, keys held). Go-Explore reached a mean of 238 rooms and 9.1 levels, in about half the frames of the downscaled version. Best single robustified run: 18,003,200 points, 1,441 levels, 6,198,985 frames (28.7 hours of play).
numbers: Exploration averages over 50 runs. The human world record is 1,219,200, so the best run is over ten times that. The default game time limit of 400,000 frames was lifted for that run.
limits: A few cells of domain knowledge (keys, room) gave large gains. The score is limited by the game clock, not the method.
agent_relevance: A tiny hand-made state descriptor (what we hold, where we are) beat raw-pixel similarity. For our schema: describe states by a few task facts, not by text similarity.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019, v4 2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Pitfall. Without domain knowledge the downscaled version found 22 rooms and no positive reward. With domain knowledge (room, x, y) Phase 1 visited 40 rooms and collected a mean of 70,264 points (CI 67,287 to 73,150). Abstract: first to score above 0 under stochastic testing, almost 60,000 after robustification.
numbers: Maximum possible about 112,000. Full-length Pitfall trajectories were hard to robustify because the network had no memory of past rooms.
limits: Pitfall is deceptive: only 32 positive rewards and many small negative ones.
agent_relevance: The archive keeps working after reward stops arriving: it keeps replacing a cell trajectory with higher-scoring ones. Useful in sparse-reward tasks.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Nature version. Go-Explore beats the state of the art on all 11 hard-exploration and unsolved Atari games (Freeway tie) and exceeds average human score on all of them, under sticky actions. The exploration phase alone exceeds human score on every one of the 55 Atari games with the downscaled cells.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: robustified mean 1,731,645 (150 times previous SOTA; above the human record 1.2M). Pitfall: mean 102,571 (max about 112,000). Private Eye: highest possible score in 4 of 5 runs. Go-Explore beats Agent57 on 7 of 11 games, using 30B frames (40B on Solaris) against 100B.
limits: Agent57 was tested without sticky actions, so the comparison is not like for like. Frames skipped by restoring simulator state are not counted.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence on a standard benchmark that returning to stored states beats mixing exploration into every episode.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Cell selection and exploration settings. A cell is chosen with probability proportional to a weight built from counts (times chosen, times visited, and how often a pick led to new cells). Exploration: 100 random actions in Atari, 30 in robotics, with 95% (Atari) or 90% (robotics) chance to repeat the last action. Batches of 100 cells explored in parallel.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge with domain knowledge adds a neighbour bonus (fewer horizontal neighbours in the archive gives higher weight), a key bonus, and a level factor 0.1 to the power (max level minus level). The authors say this greatly improves Montezuma's Revenge and has little effect on Pitfall.
limits: Selection weights were hand-designed per game. Pitfall got no gain from an analogous design.
agent_relevance: Selection rule: favour cells that are fresh, rarely tried, or that led to new cells. We can copy a count-based priority with a bonus for fresh finds. A model could replace the hand weights (see IGE).

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Downscaling parameters are tuned during the run by an objective: a target number of cells (a fixed fraction of the sample) plus the normalised entropy of how recent frames spread over cells. This avoids one cell per frame and one cell for all frames.
numbers: The term L(n,T) penalises distance from the target cell count; the entropy is divided by that of a uniform spread so values compare across cell counts.
limits: Only tested on Atari frames.
agent_relevance: A general rule for any state abstraction: keep the number of classes near a target and keep items spread evenly across classes.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Robotics test. A simulated Fetch arm must pick an object and place it on one of four shelves (two with doors). The exploration phase found a successful trajectory in 198 of 200 runs (50 per shelf; 99%), all but the two failures in under 2 billion frames. After robustification, policies placed the object in 99% of trials.
numbers: Controls: plain PPO, 5 runs per shelf, 1B frames, found no reward ever. PPO with count-based intrinsic reward on the same cells, 10 runs per shelf, 2B frames, found no reward. Cells came from MuJoCo internal state (domain knowledge).
limits: Two runs failed after 3B frames. Cells came from simulator internals.
agent_relevance: Archive plus return beats curiosity in a sparse chain of skills (touch, grasp, lift, place).

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Direct evidence for derailment in robotics. In 20 count-based intrinsic motivation control runs, all discovered touch and grasp, but in 18 (90%) the visit count of the grasp step was at least 10 times smaller than for touch. The agent kept finding the stepping stone but could not return to it reliably.
numbers: 18 of 20 runs show the 10x drop; the other 2 show a 10x drop between grasp and lift, or never found lift. The rarely visited cells should have had the highest intrinsic reward, yet they were not revisited.
limits: Counts are indirect evidence; no intervention that removes derailment was run in this analysis.
agent_relevance: Supports separate noise levels: low noise while re-entering a known good state, high noise only after arrival.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Supplementary argument on derailment. Epsilon-greedy with a small fixed epsilon avoids derailment but explores little at the frontier; annealing explores early with heavy derailment. The proposed fix is separate exploration probabilities: low in known areas, high in unknown areas.
numbers: Reasoning argument, with the Go-Explore return step as the extreme case (zero exploration while returning).
limits: An argument, not an ablation with measured effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Doubt and exploration should be gated by state: none while re-entering a stored state, strong after reaching the frontier. Matches guardrail G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Policy-based Go-Explore (no simulator restore). A goal-conditioned policy is trained to return to archive cells. With domain-knowledge cells it reached mean 97,728 on Montezuma's Revenge (about 12B frames) and 20,093 on Pitfall. Sampling from the policy found over 4 times more new cells than random actions.
numbers: Compared with the restore version it makes fewer assumptions but scores lower on Pitfall (20,093 versus 102,571 after robustification).
limits: Tested only with domain knowledge cells. The authors say a fair frame comparison with Agent57 is not possible.
agent_relevance: The archive idea survives without a perfect restore: returning is done by a policy. For an LLM, returning is re-prompting with the saved partial solution, which is exact and free.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Relation to quality-diversity. The archive is reminiscent of MAP-Elites: one best elite per cell. Difference: Go-Explore expands by extending trajectories and not by mutating policies, and cells index reachable places instead of behaviour descriptors.
numbers: No experiment compares directly with MAP-Elites.
limits: A link made in the text only. The quality-diversity subfield is covered elsewhere in this series.
agent_relevance: Cross-link to Quality-diversity and novelty search. One elite per niche is the same bookkeeping rule.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) First return, then explore. Nature 590
finding: Limits of restoring simulator state: a trajectory found by lucky actions in a stochastic world can be hard to robustify. The authors give a highway example where a direct crossing works in the simulator by luck but not in real traffic, so the safer overpass route is missed.
numbers: Written example, no numbers. Also: the ALE score overflows at 1M points and a last-life bug had to be patched.
limits: The authors recommend robustification and policy-based returns to close the gap.
agent_relevance: Archive-held solutions must be re-tested under variation before use (guardrail G3: pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Yang, Moerland, Preuss, Plaat (2022) The Benefit of Post-Exploration in Intrinsic Motivation
finding: First isolated test of the explore half of Go-Explore. Turning post-exploration (random exploring after reaching a goal) on or off inside the same goal-conditioned agent. With post-exploration the agent did better in all three MiniGrid tasks (FourRooms, LavaCrossingS11N5, LavaGapS7).
numbers: LavaCrossing and LavaGap averaged over 10 environment seeds with 5 repeats; FourRooms over three epsilon values. Post-exploration changed performance more than tuning the epsilon used while reaching the goal.
limits: Small gridworlds. Effects are shown on curves, with no exact table values in the text.
agent_relevance: Confirms that exploring after arriving is a separate lever from exploring on the way.

source: Yang, Moerland, Preuss, Plaat (2022) The Benefit of Post-Exploration in Intrinsic Motivation
finding: Adaptive post-exploration. Post-explore with a probability that falls with how often the goal was visited (novelty as a sign of the border). Small decay rates (0.01 and 0.05) slightly beat always post-exploring; a full decay rate of 1 clearly hurt. Duration, fixed 20 steps or a share of the goal-reaching length, was about equal on learning curves.
numbers: The percentage-based duration did better on the relabelling analysis. Setting a new goal after arrival was not equal to post-exploration, because the next goal pulls the agent back into known ground.
limits: Effect sizes are small and seen on FourRooms curves only.
agent_relevance: Spend extra exploration only at the border of what is known. Skip it when the state is already well visited.

source: Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore (2022, v3 2023)
finding: Removes hand-built cells. States are embedded in a learned latent space; a final goal is chosen from low-density latent regions; the agent follows a subgoal trajectory and then explores. On a continuous maze only LGE and Go-Explore clearly beat random exploration; curiosity (ICM, surprise), Skew-Fit and DIAYN were not clearly better than random.
numbers: LGE covered almost all reachable maze space. In the robot arm task (10 runs each) Go-Explore with a naive grid cell was only slightly better than random; LGE was clearly better. On Atari (3 runs each) LGE slightly beat Go-Explore on Pitfall and Montezuma, yet found far fewer cells than full Go-Explore with domain knowledge (about 5k cells on Montezuma).
limits: Needs the same initial state every episode. Goal-reached test is a latent distance threshold. Atari runs are short and few.
agent_relevance: Shows the cell design is the weak point: a naive grid can erase the benefit. A learned similarity works, but domain knowledge still wins on Atari.

source: Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore (2022, v3 2023)
finding: Ablations on the maze: removing post-goal exploration, removing low-density goal sampling, or removing the subgoal trajectory each gave a significant drop. Exploration after reaching the goal was crucial; conditioning on successive subgoals greatly helped.
numbers: Three ablations on one maze, interquartile means with 95% intervals.
limits: One environment for ablations.
agent_relevance: Replicates the post-exploration finding and adds that following the stored path stepwise helps more than aiming at the end state only.

source: Time-Myopic Go-Explore: learning a state representation for the Go-Explore paradigm (2023, NeurIPS DRL workshop)
finding: Learns an embedding where temporally close states cluster, and adds a state to the archive only if it is far in predicted time from every existing cell. Matches native Go-Explore at 1M frames on Gravitar and Montezuma-level scores at 5M, trails it on Frostbite.
numbers: Mean reward, 20 runs: Montezuma 695 at 1M frames and 2,090 at 5M versus native Go-Explore 2,303 at 1M; Gravitar 2,533 (1M) and 3,161 (5M) versus native 2,130; Frostbite 3,543 and 4,476 versus native 11,721.
limits: Query time grows non-linearly with archive size. Workshop paper. Native Go-Explore used the official downscaling tuned for Montezuma.
agent_relevance: A learned notion of closeness can keep the archive small without hand design.

source: Time-Myopic Go-Explore: learning a state representation for the Go-Explore paradigm (2023, NeurIPS DRL workshop)
finding: Archive bloat in native Go-Explore. In Montezuma at scores 100, 400, 500 and 2500 the native archive held 126, 198, 1,812 and 2,839 cells; the time-myopic archive held 160, 203, 450 and 566 (setting L=20). On Gravitar after 1M frames: 7,376 native cells versus 381, with a higher score.
numbers: Means over 20 runs.
limits: The authors say the native archive explodes after score 400; the cause is not tested.
agent_relevance: Archives grow with noise. Merge near-duplicates or the choice step gets diluted.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: Replaces all three hand heuristics of Go-Explore with a language model: choose which archive state to return to, choose the next action, and decide whether a new state is interestingly new enough for the archive. Archive of text states; return by restoring the environment.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 hard problems): 100% success within 150 operations, on average 70.8% faster than the next best baseline (depth-first search). Tree of Thoughts reference 74%. Cost per task about 1.04 USD (Game of 24) and 2.01 USD (BabyAI); total under 2,000 USD.
quote: In Coin Collector, IGE is the only method that can find the solution in the maze
limits: The model picks from valid options in Game of 24, so it is not comparable with ToT. Needs resettable environments.
agent_relevance: Closest published design to our need: an archive of promising partial states and a model that picks, extends and filters. Our program should hold the archive and counts; the model fills slots.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: TextWorld, 25 seeds, 240 steps. Cooking Game: IGE 92% versus ReAct 56%, Reflexion 52%, naive LLM 40%, random 0%. Coin Collector: IGE 88%, all others 0%. Treasure Hunter: IGE 96% versus ReAct 84%, Reflexion 80%, naive 64%, random 0%.
numbers: Chi-square gap significant (p<0.05) on the two harder games. BFS-like behaviour appeared: the model picks rooms with unexplored exits and removes exhausted rooms.
limits: Values read from the figure labels. 25 seeds per game.
agent_relevance: Removing exhausted states from the archive is what produced search-like behaviour from a model.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: BabyAI with 250 environment steps. Text, Put Next To: IGE 84% versus ReAct 48% (a 36 point gain, significant); Open Door 64% equal to the best other. Vision (GPT-4o images), Put Next To: 52% versus 8% for ReAct; Open Door 8% versus 0%. The RL-trained GLAM baseline needed 1.5M online steps (4% on Put Next To).
numbers: 25 seeds per task type. Reflexion omitted in BabyAI for cost.
limits: Open Door in vision is still only 8%.
agent_relevance: An archive search let a model do in 250 steps what RL needed 1.5 million for. The gap grows with difficulty.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: Ablation, success rate, in the order Game of 24 / BabyAI Put Next To / TextWorld Cooking. Full IGE 100 / 84 / 92. Without model action choice 68 / 24 / 0. Without model state choice 96 / 48 / 76. Without model archive filter 93 / 64 / 64. All three removed 61 / 4 / 0. Without per-state action history 33 / 72 / 72. Classic Go-Explore (visit-frequency weights, random actions) 38 / 4 / 0.
numbers: Bootstrap 95% intervals, for example 84 +/- 14 and 92 +/- 10 for IGE on the two longer tasks; 25 seeds (100 on Game of 24).
limits: Column order checked against the raw text extraction of the table.
agent_relevance: Each step carries weight, and which one matters depends on horizon: action diversity for short horizon, state selection and filtering for long horizon. Random actions (classic Go-Explore) collapse in text tasks.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: Other models on Game of 24, success: GPT-4 naive 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83, IGE 100. Llama-3 400B: 44, 68, 54, IGE 98. Claude Sonnet 3.5: 24, 58, 80, IGE 86 (not significantly above Reflexion at 80).
numbers: Bootstrap intervals, for example Claude IGE 86 +/- 9 and Reflexion 80 +/- 11.
limits: One task, three models.
agent_relevance: The gain is largest over the weaker baselines. With a strong reflection method (Claude Reflexion) the gap nearly closes.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: Model-based archive filtering keeps the archive small. Without it the archive was over 5 times larger in BabyAI and TextWorld. Reflexion did not beat ReAct in TextWorld, which the authors link to long episode histories; IGE controls context by pruning states.
numbers: Mean states: BabyAI Put Next To 203.5 +/- 56.7 versus 25.5 +/- 5.2 with filter; Cooking Game 22.4 +/- 15.3 versus 4.4 +/- 2.8 (column mapping inferred from the text claim of over 5 times); Game of 24 18.5 versus 15.6.
limits: The Reflexion explanation is a hypothesis in the paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a pruned archive and short context. Fits G7 (every element must pay for itself).

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models. ICLR
finding: Prompt robustness: with domain-general prompts (no hints) Game of 24 reached 96% against 100% with tuned prompts, and still beat the baselines. Malformed model outputs were under 0.1% of actions.
numbers: Appendix table 5; same evaluation setting as the ablation.
limits: Similar trends were reported for BabyAI Put Next To and the Cooking Game.
agent_relevance: The archive loop is not very sensitive to prompt wording. Good for a scaffold.

source: Bhatt, Wood, Habler, Al-Kahfah (2026) Large Empirical Case Study: Go-Explore adapted for AI Red Team Testing
finding: Go-Explore applied to find prompt-injection attacks on GPT-4o-mini (28 runs, 6 research questions). Seed variance dominated: across 5 seeds the number of findings ranged 0 to 16 (8 times spread). Tools-only state signature averaged 1.8 +/- 1.3 findings, full-intent 4.6 +/- 6.0, with no consistent winner.
numbers: Averaging 3 to 4 seeds stabilised the cumulative mean in their one ordering (seed 42 gave 16 against a 4.6 mean). Most other research questions used a single seed (42).
limits: Preprint, one model. The authors say 70 to 90 percent of findings were false positives. Most comparisons are single-seed.
agent_relevance: One run of an archive search is not evidence. Use several seeds when comparing archive variants.

source: Bhatt, Wood, Habler, Al-Kahfah (2026) Large Empirical Case Study: Go-Explore adapted for AI Red Team Testing
finding: Failure of reward shaping in an LLM archive search. Causality bonus rewards collapsed exploration by 94% (161 findings, 847 tool calls) with granular signatures; alone they gave 18 false positives and 0 verified attacks; all three enhancements together gave zero findings. Safety refusals collapsed 96% of attack intents into one cell.
numbers: Targeted prompts alone found 1 attack in 13 findings. An ensemble of agents found more attack types but fewer of each type.
limits: Single seed for these comparisons, so the seed warning applies to them too.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: when a model refuses, state signatures collapse and the archive degenerates. Reward bonuses on an archive can amplify noise.

source: Adaptive Stress Testing without Domain Heuristics using Go-Explore (2020)
finding: Go-Explore transferred to failure search for an autonomous car with a crossing pedestrian. Cells are indexed by a hash of step number and discretised action, so no simulator state is needed; return is by replaying the action history. Without a heuristic reward, the DRL solver found no failure on the medium and hard scenarios.
numbers: Three scenarios (easy, medium, hard; horizon 50, 50, 100 steps), 100 iterations each. Medium: MCTS beat Go-Explore at short horizon. Hard (long horizon): neither DRL nor MCTS found a failure; Go-Explore did, and Go-Explore plus backward algorithm improved it. Easy, with heuristic reward: DRL best, Go-Explore worst.
limits: Comparison is on the likelihood of the failure found, one scenario family, 100 iterations.
agent_relevance: Archive search wins when reward gives no guidance and the chain is long; plain search wins at short horizon. Use the archive for long chains only.

source: Salimans and Chen (2018) Learning Montezuma's Revenge from a Single Demonstration
finding: Formal reason why returning to stored states helps. On a toy blind cliff walk with N states between rewards, standard RL needs time that grows exponentially in N (about 2 to the N random steps to see a reward). Starting each episode from a state on a demonstration and moving the start backward makes the cost about quadratic in N. This is the basis of Go-Explore robustification.
numbers: Toy cliff walk: geometric means over 20 seeds, policy gradient to 95% solve rate. Montezuma's Revenge: high score 74,500, above all earlier published results at that time (it beat the demonstrator score of 71,500).
limits: Needs a restorable emulator and one good demonstration. The game is deterministic and noise levels differ between papers, so scores are hard to compare.
agent_relevance: Strongest theory for an archive: a stored path turns an exponential search into a sum of short searches. Our version: re-start from the last verified step, not from the beginning.

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents. ICLR
finding: An archive of coding agents used as stepping stones, in the Go-Explore spirit. Parents are sampled from the whole archive, roughly in proportion to score and in inverse proportion to the number of children, with non-zero chance for every agent. Only agents that compile and can still edit code enter the archive. Children are scored on benchmark logs.
numbers: 80 iterations. SWE-bench (verified subset) 20.0% to 50.0%; Polyglot (50-task subset) 14.0% to 38.0%, and 14.2% to 30.7% on the full Polyglot. Ablations (SWE-bench / Polyglot): no open-ended archive 23.0% / 14.0%; no self-improvement 39.0% / 28.0%; greedy parent choice 39.7% / 30.0%.
limits: One run per arm as reported in Table 1; benchmark subsets small (50 Polyglot tasks). Agents run with Claude 3.5 Sonnet or o3-mini.
agent_relevance: Direct test of keep-the-whole-archive versus keep-the-latest versus keep-the-best: greedy lost about 10 points to the archive. Two score dips (iterations 4 and 56) later led to the best agents. Supports keeping non-best partial solutions.
